title: Ivo and the Songbook
premise: Quentin Nystrom, a cellist whose career ended in a humiliating collapse at her final conservatory performance, retreats to a fading coastal town and takes work restoring an old hotel's library. There she is assigned, anonymously, to correspond with another guest as part of the owner's eccentric winter tradition — only to discover her pen pal is Ivo Marchetti, the conductor whose review destroyed her. Through letters neither knows the other's identity, they fall into honesty; when the truth surfaces, Quentin must choose between the revenge she's planned and the justice of telling her own story aloud. In the end she performs again — not for vindication, but because staying invisible costs more than failing ever did.
about_author: Juniper Coldharbour is the pen name of a former orchestra librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing her own stories. She lives in a drafty house by the sea with a dog named Fermata.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Quentin arrives in Greywater Bay on the final train of the season, fleeing a career that ended mid-phrase at her conservatory debut. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: numb relief — she has chosen invisibility and tells herself it feels like peace.

chapters.title: Salt and Dust
chapters.summary: Settling into the decaying Hotel Meridian, Quentin takes a job restoring its flooded library and meets the formidable owner, Mrs. Aldous, who announces the annual anonymous winter correspondence between guests. POV: Quentin. Beat: wary curiosity; the town notices her cello case and she lies about it.

chapters.title: Correspondent Unknown
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous assigns pen pals by lottery. Quentin draws 'I.M.' and writes a guarded first letter; across the hotel, Ivo Marchetti — the critic-conductor whose review gutted her — receives hers without knowing who wrote it. POV: alternating. Beat: dramatic irony established; both are performing versions of themselves.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Restoring water-damaged books, Quentin finds a songbook from 1946 inscribed to a woman who vanished from the hotel. She begins researching the story as a distraction. POV: Quentin. Beat: quiet obsession; the past offers a safer mystery than her own life.

chapters.title: Letters Without Faces
chapters.summary: The correspondence deepens: 'I.M.' confesses he once destroyed someone with words and has never forgiven himself. Quentin, recognizing nothing yet, answers with her own account of public ruin. POV: alternating letters. Beat: intimacy through anonymity; each believes the other is safe.

chapters.title: The Man in the Lobby
chapters.summary: Quentin encounters Ivo Marchetti in person — arrogant, wounded, recently disgraced himself after walking out on his own orchestra. They clash spectacularly over dinner. POV: Quentin. Beat: hostility sharpened by unacknowledged recognition of something familiar in him.

chapters.title: Fermata
chapters.summary: Snowed in, the guests are forced together. Ivo hears Quentin humming a phrase from the piece she failed at and freezes — he knows it. He says nothing. POV: Ivo. Beat: guilt ignites; he suspects his pen pal and his enemy may be the same woman.

chapters.title: The Songbook's Second Verse
chapters.summary: Quentin discovers the 1946 songbook belonged to a cellist who was driven out of the hotel by a false accusation — and that Mrs. Aldous was her friend. The parallel to her own story unsettles her. POV: Quentin. Beat: inheritance of injustice; history rhymes.

chapters.title: Two Handwritings
chapters.summary: Ivo tests his theory by slipping a musical quotation into a letter. Quentin recognizes the phrase — the one from his devastating review — and realizes who her correspondent is. POV: Quentin. Beat: vertigo; every tender letter now reads as betrayal.

chapters.title: What I Would Say to You
chapters.summary: Quentin keeps writing anyway, weaponizing the anonymity: probing, needling, watching him squirm at breakfast. But his answers grow more honest than any apology she imagined. POV: Quentin. Beat: revenge curdling into confusion — cruelty isn't landing the way she planned.

chapters.title: The Review
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: the night of Quentin's catastrophic performance, her panic attack onstage, and Ivo's printed evisceration the next morning — written while grieving his father, a truth no one asked for. POV: Ivo. Beat: sympathy shifts; the villain becomes legible.

chapters.title: Thaw Lines
chapters.summary: Forced to collaborate on the hotel's solstice concert, Quentin and Ivo rehearse together, sniping, then playing well. The letters continue in parallel, each hiding what the rehearsals reveal. POV: alternating. Beat: grudging duet; attraction stops being deniable.

chapters.title: Confession in C Minor
chapters.summary: After rehearsal, Ivo nearly tells Quentin he's her pen pal but loses his nerve; instead he confesses in a letter that he's falling for someone in the hotel. Quentin reads it hours after laughing with him. POV: Quentin. Beat: heartbreak ahead of schedule; she decides to end the correspondence.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Quentin drafts a brutal farewell revealing everything — then can't send it. Instead she plays the songbook's recovered melody alone in the library, unaware Ivo is listening from the stairwell. POV: Ivo. Beat: he finally understands who she is, entirely.

chapters.title: Last Train Out
chapters.summary: A storm cancels trains; Mrs. Aldous falls ill and asks them jointly to organize the solstice concert. Trapped together with a deadline, Quentin and Ivo negotiate an armed truce. POV: alternating. Beat: proximity as pressure; the price of survival means needing people.

chapters.title: What the Songbook Owed Her
chapters.summary: Quentin and Mrs. Aldous clear the name of the 1946 cellist, presenting evidence to the town — justice outside any court. Watching the town listen, Quentin wonders if her own story could be told the same way. POV: Quentin. Beat: hope with teeth; testimony as repair.

chapters.title: Intermission
chapters.summary: On the eve of the concert, Ivo leaves a letter unsigned but unmistakable: a full confession of the review, his grief, and his love. Quentin burns it unread — then retrieves it from the grate. POV: Quentin. Beat: climax of internal conflict; she cannot unknow what she almost refused to read.

chapters.title: Solstice
chapters.summary: The concert. Quentin takes the stage for the first time since her collapse, plays the songbook melody, and publicly claims her own failure and return. Ivo follows with a spoken apology before the whole town. POV: alternating. Beat: climax; visibility chosen over safety.

chapters.title: After the Applause
chapters.summary: Alone afterward, they finally speak without paper between them — anger, grief, and the raw fact of having hurt each other honestly. No instant forgiveness; only the decision to keep talking. POV: Quentin. Beat: aftermath; love as ongoing labor, not absolution.

chapters.title: The Price of Staying
chapters.summary: Spring approaches; Ivo is offered his orchestra back and Quentin a teaching post far away. Both must decide whether second chances require leaving. POV: alternating. Beat: rising stakes of ordinary life; the last train metaphor returns.

chapters.title: Someone Stays
chapters.summary: Ivo declines the orchestra to lead the town's small ensemble; Quentin accepts the post but commutes — or rather, they build a life between two stations. The songbook is formally donated under its true owner's name. POV: Quentin. Beat: resolution; inheritance honored, futures chosen.

chapters.title: Coda: First Train
chapters.summary: One year later, the new season's first train arrives carrying new guests. Mrs. Aldous hands Quentin the pen-pal lottery box; she and Ivo write one final joint letter to a stranger, beginning 'We were enemies first.' POV: Quentin. Beat: full-circle warmth; the tradition continues, transformed.
